# The Process of Individuation

The concept of individuation designates the process by which a person becomes a psychological individual, that is, a separate, indivisible unity or whole. It is the development of the psychological individual as a being distinct from the general, collective psychology. Individuation, therefore, is a process of differentiation, having for its goal the development of the individual personality.

Individuation means becoming an individual, and, in so far as individuality embraces our innermost, last, and incomparable uniqueness, it also implies becoming one's own self. We could therefore translate individuation as coming to selfhood or self-realization. The self is not only the centre but also the whole circumference which embraces both conscious and unconscious; it is the centre of this totality, just as the ego is the centre of consciousness.

The goal of individuation is nothing less than to divest the self of the false wrappings of the persona on the one hand, and of the suggestive power of primordial images on the other. Integration of the personality is achieved when the individual has confronted, acknowledged, and assimilated the various components of the psyche: the shadow, the anima or animus, and ultimately the self. This wholeness is not a state of perfection but of completeness, embracing both light and dark.

The natural process of individuation brings to birth a consciousness of human community precisely because it makes us aware of the unconscious, which unites and is common to all mankind. Individuation does not shut one out from the world, but gathers the world to oneself. The development of personality means fidelity to the law of one's own being.
